title: From Prediction to Wisdom: The Epistemic Imperative in AI World Models
content: Contemporary AI development is deeply rooted in a "computationalist paradigm" grounded in the intellectual legacies of Turing, Shannon, and McCulloch and Pitts. This paradigm treats symbolic manipulation, signal statistics, and neural activation as the essence of intelligence, expecting that injecting ever-greater volumes of data and computational resources (compute) will eventually cause genuine intelligence to emerge. This paper argues that the optimism of the "scaling law" thesis overlooks a fundamental problem: the structural deficiency whereby AI systems lack a Theory of Knowledge. This argument is developed from multiple perspectives spanning philosophy, information science, and cognitive science. The paper advances three central claims. First, prediction is not knowledge, and simulation is not understanding. Second, genuine intelligence requires a "coherence architecture" comprising persistent memory, causal constraint, self-governance, and non-Markovian reasoning. Third, Burgin's General Theory of Information (GTI), Mikkilineni's Mindful Machine thesis, Maturana and Varela's autopoiesis, Deutsch's constructor theory, and the existential philosophy of Heidegger and Arendt together supply an integrated theoretical framework capable of addressing this deficiency. The paper further argues that the "Coherence Debt" embedded in the current AI boom risks a catastrophic misallocation of energy and capital, and makes the case for the epistemic necessity of a transition to Mindful Machines.
